title: The Role of Stock Exchanges in Promoting the Banking Sector in Adopting Green Finance
text:
Abstract
This study investigates how stock exchanges can promote green finance adoption among banks globally. It combines a synthesis of 64 sources with primary survey data from financial practitioners across emerging markets including India, Malaysia, Ghana and Sri Lanka, and identifies four interdependent drivers of adoption, namely market regulations, market mechanisms, awareness and incentives. IMF/IOSCO data show that only 49% of regulators in low-income economies maintain supportive market regulations, compared with 85% in high-income OECD nations. The findings indicate that stock exchanges must move from voluntary guidance to binding frameworks that mandate ESG disclosure and green bond standards for listed banks, supported by targeted tax incentives, formal peer exchange partnerships and standardised carbon market disclosure.








Figure 1. Share of securities regulators maintaining market regulations that support green finance, by income group (IMF/IOSCO data as reported in the paper). Drawn in R.

title: The Role of Stock Exchanges in Promoting the Banking Sector in Adopting Green Finance
text:
Data and code
The survey behind the paper has 103 respondents and 30 five-point Likert items covering market regulations, market mechanisms, awareness, incentives and green finance adoption. The item-level data, the SPSS data file and the original SPSS output are public on Figshare. A companion repository re-runs the analysis in R and Quarto, with an independent Python/Jupyter audit of the same files and a direct reconciliation against the SPSS data.

title: The Role of Stock Exchanges in Promoting the Banking Sector in Adopting Green Finance
text:
Policy frameworks
The paper’s main policy contribution is a set of SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound) implementation frameworks for closing the gap in green finance adoption between banks listed on high-income, well-regulated exchanges and those in low- and middle-income markets. The four tables below are generated in R from a data file.



Table 8. SMART framework for the relationship between regulations and green finance adoption. Source: Author.




Criteria


Implementation plan






Specific


Mandate climate risk disclosure rules for all licensed banks, with annual reporting of financed emissions (Scope 3) and public disclosure of green asset ratios (GAR) by Q2 2028.




Measurable


100% compliance with disclosure rules by Q2 2028; 40% of bank portfolios allocated to green/social financing loans by Q3 2029; penalties for non-compliance (e.g. 1.5% of revenue for missed targets).




Achievable


Central bank adoption of ECB-linked climate stress tests; SEC alignment with regional ESG disclosure standards (e.g. ASEAN); technical assistance from the IMF’s Climate Finance Task Force.




Relevant


Linked to IPCC 1.5°C pathways (e.g. 40% emissions cuts in transport/buildings by 2030).




Time-bound


Phase 1 (Q4 2026), draft regulations finalised. Phase 2 (Q4 2027), pilot with systemically important banks. Phase 3 (Q4 2028), full enforcement.








Table 9. SMART framework for the relationship between market mechanisms and green finance adoption. Source: Author.




Criteria


Implementation plan






Specific


Establish a Green Finance Task Force at emerging-economy stock exchanges to implement the UN SSE Carbon Market Framework and require every bank to list a green financial product by 2030.




Measurable


10+ certified green bonds listed by Q2 2028; pilot carbon credit trading platform launched by Q3 2028 with national government.




Achievable


Leverage partnerships with the SEC, Ministry of Environment, MDBs and national government through MOUs.




Relevant


Aligned with updated NDCs, 2050 Net Zero roadmaps, and UN SDGs 7, 12 and 13.




Time-bound


Phase 1 (Q4 2027), updated regulatory framework. Phase 2 (Q1 2028), market readiness assessment. Phase 3 (Q2 2029), full implementation.








Table 10. SMART framework for the relationship between market awareness and green finance adoption. Source: Author.




Criteria


Implementation plan






Specific


Formalise co-regional technology transfer mechanisms between emerging and developed economies (e.g. Colombo Stock Exchange and Singapore Stock Exchange) via working groups on green bond listings and carbon market integration.




Measurable


Adoption of 3 developed-economy-aligned ESG policies within the first 12 months.




Achievable


Leverage UN SSE partnerships with global exchanges for funding and technical support.




Relevant


Aligned with the domestic national climate strategy (2023-2030) and updated NDC targets.




Time-bound


Phase 1 (Q3 2026), policy drafting. Phase 2 (Q1 2027), launch. Phase 3 (Q1 2028), regional expansion.








Table 11. SMART framework for the relationship between incentives and green finance adoption. Source: Author.




Criteria


Implementation plan






Specific


Targeted incentives for energy, low-carbon buildings, transport, and land use (rainforest conservation, soil enrichment), with 20% of bank portfolios directed to these sectors by 2028.




Measurable


30% of listed entities adopting IPCC 1.5°C-aligned transition plans by 2027.




Achievable


Collaboration between the Securities Exchange Commission and Departments of Inland Revenue on tax breaks for green bonds.




Relevant


Aligned with UNFCCC Article 6 carbon trading and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development.




Time-bound


Phase 1 (Q1 2028), pilot tax breaks. Phase 2 (Q1 2029), expand green bond issuance to 35% of listed bond issuances.

title: Cost of capital, energy adoption and integrated assessment
text:
Research / Statements / Cost of capital, energy adoption and integrated assessment


Research statement for the PhD programme in Environmental Economics, Yale School of the Environment, Fall 2027. Written with reference to the work of Professor Kenneth Gillingham.



My MSc dissertation at London Metropolitan University asked why climate finance reaches so few of the places that need it. It ended with a theoretical contribution I call the Institutional Reinforcement Cycle (IRC). I want to spend my doctoral years at Yale turning the IRC from a framework I believe in into something a skeptical economist would accept. That means writing it down formally, estimating it, and finding out where it fails.
The IRC treats a climate finance system as a product of its components rather than a sum. Institutional collaboration, policy alignment, blended finance deployment and transparency compound, so a value near zero on one of them can stall the whole system however much capital sits in the funds. My evidence so far is a survey of 103 climate finance professionals and eight interviews with practitioners at UNDP, UNCDF, UN Sustainable Stock Exchanges, FAO, the African Development Bank, the Asian Development Bank, the World Bank GEF, a central bank and a private capital firm. It points to institutional collaboration, rather than the volume of blended finance, as the binding constraint. I presented this at the 3rd International Conference on Biomimicry for Sustainability in August 2026, and the paper is now under revision at Climate and Development. A survey of this size motivates the multiplicative form but does not identify it, and getting to an estimable, identified specification is the first thing I would like to work on with you.
The first direction connects the IRC to integrated assessment modeling, and your recent work, Professor Gillingham, gave me the most to think about here. In your Annual Review of Economics survey with Jesús Fernández-Villaverde and Simon Scheidegger, you note that IAM conclusions depend heavily on parameter values and functional forms. You also describe how deep equilibrium nets make uncertainty quantification feasible on models that were once too costly to solve repeatedly. IAMs typically treat the cost of capital in developing economies as an exogenous parameter. The IRC suggests it is partly an outcome of the institutional architecture around those markets. I would like to estimate that relationship from data and add it to a structural IAM as a regional wedge in the cost of capital. I would then use surrogate model methods to ask how much of the uncertainty in mitigation feasibility for G77 economies traces back to institutional quality rather than to technology or damages. The first year theory and econometrics sequence, and time with your group, are where I intend to build the structural modeling skills this needs.
The second direction is closer to your empirical work on energy technology. My layered capital structure has a concessional first loss tranche, a multilateral guarantee mezzanine and a household deposit senior tranche. It is meant to lower the cost of capital for decentralized clean energy, where financing cost is a large share of the price households face. Your paper with Todd Gerarden, Bryan Bollinger and Daniel Xu on solar tariffs is a model I want to learn from. It finds that a subsidy that does not discriminate by origin beats a targeted one, because each public dollar goes further when it supports lower cost production, and it reaches that result with a structural model disciplined by real data. Your work with Bollinger and Justin Kirkpatrick on valuing solar subsidies sharpens the targeting question. You find implicit discount rates of 15.3 percent for low-wealth households against 10.0 percent for high-wealth ones, and the gap persists even among households with prime credit. That makes the cost of capital one component of the adoption gap, and it gives my structure a clear test. I want to measure how much of that gap a lower cost of capital can close, and what else has to go with it. Dr. Pradeep Kurukulasuriya at UNCDF pressed the same issue from the supply side, with data showing that most multilateral development finance never reaches the highest-risk markets.
There is also a smaller project where carbon credit design meets EV adoption, and I have not found a paper on it. Verra’s VM0038 methodology issues credits for electric vehicle charging systems based on the fossil fuel emissions they displace. It ties eligibility and additionality to how far EV adoption has progressed in a market. I worked with this methodology while structuring the carbon programme at Kangara Holdings, where EV charging centres are one component. Your work with Marten Ovaere and Stephanie Weber on carbon policy and the emissions implications of electric vehicles speaks directly to whether such credits measure what they claim to. I would like to ask whether credit rules keyed to market share thresholds distort where charging capacity gets built.
What I bring is field experience and access. In 2025 I wrote Sri Lanka’s expression of interest to the Climate Investment Funds’ Industry Decarbonization Program, so I have seen from the inside how concessional finance for industry is designed and allocated in a developing economy. Your Science piece with Lint Barrage calls for more economic quantification of industrial decarbonization and industrial policy. A developing country view of concessional finance is where I could contribute to that agenda. I have also sat across the table from rice farmers in Sri Lanka’s dry zone while we negotiated an agricultural carbon credit agreement. Before that meeting I had run the additionality test myself with the government, a difference in differences comparison of adopters and nonadopters of the proposed practice changes, checking whether each intervention exceeded VM0042’s 5 percent quantitative change threshold and whether regional adoption stayed below the 20 percent common practice ceiling. The farmers were not worried about methodology. They wanted to know what happens to their land rights if the project outlasts the company that signed it. That is a moral hazard and enforcement problem inside blended finance, and I want the tools to model it rather than describe it.
To keep the work tied to data, I plan to run a small pilot with a commercial bank in a Small Island Developing State during the doctorate. My relationships with Dr. Kurukulasuriya, Jason Spensley at the World Bank GEF and Dr. Anthony Miller at UN Sustainable Stock Exchanges make this possible without large seed capital. Their feedback on my early model complicated it usefully. Mr. Spensley, for one, thought the mechanism technically feasible but politically uncertain. The pilot’s purpose is to produce real pricing, take-up and default data under a guarantee. I could then use that data to discipline the model’s parameters and see where the structure breaks.
This work sits inside a wider programme with three strands, the capital structure itself, its application to energy and its application to regenerative agriculture, which my personal statement describes. I have attended three UNFCCC COPs and two UNCCD COPs, and in those rooms the gap between capital pledged and capital deployed was the most consistent problem I saw. The energy and IAM strands of this programme need the empirical and modeling discipline of your group, Professor Gillingham, and I want to find out early where my framework holds and where it breaks.

title: Statement of purpose
text:
Research / Statements / Statement of purpose


Statement of purpose for the PhD programme in Environmental Economics, Yale School of the Environment, Fall 2027.



My paternal grandfather spent his life at sea to put two meals on his family’s table. My maternal grandfather farmed paddy with eight children and no means to send my mother past secondary school. I did not inherit their poverty. What I inherited was a question. Why does capital that could change families like mine sit idle, thousands of miles away, in banks that will never lend to them? That question has organized my academic and professional life. It is what I want a PhD to help me answer rigorously.
I began at the edges of it. My BSc thesis at London Metropolitan University tested four drivers of bank green finance adoption (regulation, mechanisms, awareness, and incentives) across emerging-market exchanges; Colombo’s own 15-year gap before its first green bond became the clearest example of what a missing driver costs. My MSc thesis moved from a single exchange to the full architecture of multilateral climate finance, using a 103-respondent survey, multiple regression and eight practitioner interviews to analyze blended finance and institutional collaboration among MDBs, central banks, and private capital across the G77 and China. Both projects kept pointing to the same constraint, a shortage of institutions able to move capital toward investments whose returns are slow, uncertain, or politically inconvenient.
That is the puzzle I hope to formalize as a dissertation, though the work will be finding where my framework is wrong. The three hypotheses apply one instrument to different assets. I am engineering a single layered capital structure, with concessional grants held as a standing first-loss tranche instead of a one-off transfer, multilateral guarantees as mezzanine credit enhancement, and household or bank deposits as a senior tranche. Because the grant and the guarantee absorb losses first, the senior tranche is exposed only to losses beyond them. With credible guarantees, its required return should approach the risk-free rate, compressing the institutional cost of capital that integrated assessment models treat as exogenous. The question is whether that compression survives across cash flows, from a structured note coupon to a grid tariff to a carbon credit stream, and whether it saves more than the grant costs.
My first hypothesis is that central-bank-regulated climate deposits should ease two frictions, where guarantees must reveal true risk tolerance and lenders cannot verify project quality. My second extends the logic to energy economics. Anchored guarantees can lower the cost of capital for decentralized green grids, which I would test by comparing financing terms for guaranteed and unguaranteed grid projects. My third turns to regenerative agriculture. Carbon-credit-enhanced practices, held in the structure, can become investable assets across the G77, China, and US rangelands.
The first chapter formalizes the structure as a mechanism design problem; the other two test its predictions in energy and agriculture. As an initial valuation exercise, I have priced an S&P ESG-linked knock-in call embedded in a green structured note using Black-Scholes. Its complete-markets, log-normal assumptions break under climate risk, so I want to extend that valuation to incomplete markets, in Python, R, and Stata.
Over the past year I discussed an early version of this model with Dr. Pradeep Kurukulasuriya, Executive Secretary of UNCDF; Jason Spensley, Senior Climate Change Specialist at the GEF, World Bank Group; and Dr. Anthony Miller, Chief Coordinator of UN Sustainable Stock Exchanges. Dr. Kurukulasuriya pushed me to treat how capital is raised and where it ends up going as linked problems. Mr. Spensley judged the mechanism technically feasible but politically uncertain. Dr. Miller’s account of the MDB-financed solar plant near Aswan, closed to Egyptian investors, showed how development finance can bypass local markets. I intend to keep these relationships as a reality check on my designs.
As Head of Impact Investments and Sustainability at Kangara Holdings, I sat across the table from rice farmers in Sri Lanka’s dry zone negotiating a carbon credit agreement. I had already run the additionality test with the Sri Lankan government, a difference-in-differences comparison of adopters and non-adopters of recognized regenerative practices, testing each intervention against VM0042’s practice-change and common-practice thresholds. My third hypothesis starts from that comparison. But the farmers were not worried about carbon methodology. They wanted to know what would happen to their land rights if the project outlasted the company that signed it. That conversation taught me more about moral hazard and enforcement inside blended finance than any paper I had read. It is what I want to model formally, not intuit, including the residual risk my structure cannot absorb, and who is left holding it.
I hope one of Professors Kenneth Gillingham, Eli Fenichel, or Matthew Kotchen chairs my committee, with the others as members. Professor Gillingham’s empirical work on energy technology adoption speaks directly to my second hypothesis, on what market and subsidy design gets households and utilities to adopt decentralized clean energy. Professor Fenichel’s dynamic modeling of ecological and economic systems gives me a formal way to treat financial and natural capital as stocks, the weakest part of my framework. Professor Kotchen’s research on environmental and public economics, and his multilateral development fund work, sits closest to the mechanism design questions in my first hypothesis. Professor Emeritus Robert Mendelsohn’s work valuing climate impacts on agriculture informs my third. I am applying to YSE because I need the hydrology and ecosystem courses it offers, and its applied, policy-facing seminar culture.
My MSc survey surfaced a recurring frustration. The governance of multilateral climate funds is shaped more by donor convenience than recipient need. That is why I am drawn to Yale’s Justice, Equity, Diversity, and Sustainability Initiative, whose Research Lab studies funding differences in the environmental sector. I want to ask who receives funding from multilateral climate funds, the accountability question in my dissertation.
Beyond the PhD, I want a career that institutions including UNCDF, GEF, and the World Bank’s climate funds call on for mechanism design. I want to move credibly between academic and institutional work. Rigorous ENRE training, grounded in the Economics Department’s first-year theory and econometrics sequence, is what will let me do that precisely.

title: Ravindu Nawanjana
text:
I work on climate finance in developing economies. My research asks why climate finance reaches so few of the places that need it, and how stock exchanges, multilateral climate funds and development banks, central banks and private capital can be organised to lower the cost of capital in emerging markets, the Group of 77 and China, and Small Island Developing States.
I completed an MSc in International Banking and Finance at the Guildhall School of Business and Law, London Metropolitan University, in August 2026, and I am a prospective PhD student in environmental economics. My MSc dissertation combined a survey of 103 climate finance professionals with eight interviews with practitioners at UNDP, UNCDF, UN Sustainable Stock Exchanges, FAO, the African Development Bank, the Asian Development Bank, the World Bank GEF, a central bank and a private capital firm. From that work I developed the Institutional Reinforcement Cycle, a model in which institutional collaboration, policy alignment, blended finance and transparency act as complements, so that weakness in any one of them can stall the whole system.
I do my quantitative work in R and Quarto, with Python, Stata and SPSS where a project needs them, and I keep it public. Each paper has a repository that reproduces its statistics from the survey data. Alongside research, I am Head of Impact Investments and Sustainability at Kangara Holdings in Colombo, where I work on agricultural and forestry carbon credit programmes under Verra methodologies, and I review for Economic Change and Restructuring (Springer Nature).

title: Code and data
text:
Methods toolkit
Applied quantitative methods. Linear regression and diagnostics, panel data and fixed effects, difference-in-differences, instrumental variables, regression discontinuity, correlation and reliability analysis, exploratory factor analysis, bootstrapping, survey design, DCF modelling, sensitivity analysis and evidence reconciliation.
Qualitative methods. Semi-structured expert interviews, thematic content analysis, policy analysis and institutional mapping.
Carbon markets and ESG. Verra AFOLU methodologies VM0042, VM0047 and VM0051, and VM0038 for electric vehicle charging; Project Design Document preparation; additionality assessment; GRI, SASB, TCFD, CDP and SBTi frameworks.
Software. R, Python, Quarto, Jupyter, Stata, IBM SPSS Statistics, Git and GitHub Actions. I am also working through IBM Quantum Learning coursework in Qiskit.

[Link to publication]  |  [Writing sample (PDF)]  |  [SSRN]  |  [Replication code]

title: The Role of Multilateral Climate Funds in Shaping the Architecture of Climate Finance
text:
Abstract
Multilateral climate funds (MCFs) are expected to move capital at scale into the Group of 77 (G77) and China, yet a large climate finance gap persists. Drawing on institutional economics and research on fragmented climate governance, this study examines how institutional collaboration, blended finance deployment, policy and regulatory alignment, and transparency shape the operational architecture of MCFs. It combines a survey of 103 sustainable finance specialists with eight semi-structured interviews with practitioners at multilateral development banks (MDBs) and climate funds, UN bodies, a central bank and a private capital firm. Interviewees saw blended finance as the main route to mobilising private capital, but described it as held back by fragmented governance, silos between vertical funds and MDBs, and regulatory dissonance. In the survey, institutional collaboration was the only factor with a significant, independent association with architecture effectiveness. Interviewees treated policy alignment as a precondition for absorbing capital, and transparency as the basis of investor trust. The study develops an Institutional Reinforcement Cycle, which explains why these determinants act as complements, so that weakness in one of the four can stall the whole system. It concludes that MCFs and MDBs need coordinated platforms that de-risk private investment at scale.

title: The Role of Multilateral Climate Funds in Shaping the Architecture of Climate Finance
text:
Main results, reproduced in R
The numbers below are computed when the site is built, in R, from the anonymised survey responses (103 respondents, 32 five-point Likert items) published in the study repository. Each construct is the mean of its items, and the slopes come from an OLS regression on z-scored variables. The table sets them beside the values reported from the original SPSS analysis.


R code for the scores, reliability, correlations and standardised OLS
survey <- read.csv(site_path("data", "msc", "survey_responses.csv"))
stopifnot(nrow(survey) == 103, ncol(survey) == 32, all(as.matrix(survey) %in% 1:5))

items <- list(IC = 1:7, BFD = 8:14, PRA = 15:21, TAFU = 22:28, CFA = 29:32)
scores <- as.data.frame(lapply(items, function(i) rowMeans(survey[, i])))
predictors <- c("IC", "BFD", "PRA", "TAFU")

alpha <- sapply(items, function(i) cronbach_alpha(survey[, i]))
r <- sapply(predictors, function(v) cor(scores[[v]], scores$CFA))
r_p <- sapply(predictors, function(v) cor.test(scores[[v]], scores$CFA)$p.value)
ols <- standardised_ols(scores, "CFA", predictors)

spss <- read.csv(site_path("data", "msc", "spss_published_benchmarks.csv"))
reported <- function(metric, v) spss$reported_value[spss$metric == metric & spss$construct_or_variable == v]

As an independent check, the same regression is run again in Python with NumPy’s least-squares solver on the scores R computed.


Python code for the independent least-squares check
import numpy as np

scores = np.column_stack([np.asarray(r.scores[c], dtype=float) for c in ["CFA", "IC", "BFD", "PRA", "TAFU"]])
z = (scores - scores.mean(axis=0)) / scores.std(axis=0, ddof=1)
y, X = z[:, 0], np.column_stack([np.ones(len(z)), z[:, 1:]])
beta, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)
py_betas = beta[1:].tolist()




R and Python slopes agree to within 5e-16. Rounded to three decimals, the R slopes match the SPSS-reported values exactly.


The survey numbers are associations among perception-based scores from a cross-sectional sample. They do not identify the effect of institutions on actual disbursements or emissions. The interviews explain the rest of the picture. Blended finance is seen as the main catalyst for private capital, policy alignment decides whether capital can be absorbed, and transparency sustains investor trust.

title: The Role of Multilateral Climate Funds in Shaping the Architecture of Climate Finance
The Role of Multilateral Climate Funds in Shaping the Architecture of Climate Finance
text:
Recommendations
The paper makes four recommendations. MCFs should act as coordination platforms that link MDBs, central banks and private capital providers, with joint financing platforms and shared risk-assessment matrices to cut transaction costs. Governments in the G77 and China should develop unified green finance taxonomies, enforce mandatory ESG disclosure and keep policy stable, and central banks should build climate-related financial risk into monetary and supervisory frameworks. Blended finance should be scaled through first-loss guarantees, concessional loans and targeted co-financing, particularly in climate-vulnerable SIDS and Least Developed Countries. And standardised performance indicators with verifiable impact reporting would build the investor trust the cycle depends on.

title: Climate finance as a dynamic system
text:
Research / Statements / Climate finance as a dynamic system


Research statement for the PhD programme in Environmental Economics, Yale School of the Environment, Fall 2027. Written with reference to the work of Professor Eli Fenichel.



My MSc dissertation at London Metropolitan University asked why climate finance reaches so few of the places that need it. It ended with a theoretical contribution I call the Institutional Reinforcement Cycle (IRC). I want to spend my doctoral years at Yale making the IRC rigorous, and the next step is the one your research addresses most directly, Professor Fenichel. The IRC produces system level failure from near zero values on single institutional variables. I want to treat the capital flows and the natural asset stocks that mechanism is meant to mobilize as formally interacting dynamic systems. I am currently working through capn, the natural capital valuation package you developed with Seong Do Yun and Josh Abbott, to build the numerical skills needed to model this problem as a dynamic system.
The IRC treats a climate finance system as a product of four variables rather than a sum, those being institutional collaboration, policy alignment, blended finance deployment and transparency. A near zero value on one of them collapses the system regardless of how much capital sits in the funds. My evidence so far is a survey of 103 climate finance professionals and eight interviews with practitioners at UNDP, UNCDF, UN Sustainable Stock Exchanges, FAO, the African Development Bank, the Asian Development Bank, the World Bank GEF, a central bank and a private capital firm, which points to institutional collaboration as the binding constraint. I presented this at the 3rd International Conference on Biomimicry for Sustainability in August 2026, and the paper is now under revision at Climate and Development. The survey motivates the multiplicative form. It does not identify it. Closing that gap is the first methodological problem the dissertation has to solve.
Your account of why municipalities are the frontline for climate adaptation describes, almost exactly, the kind of borrower I have been trying to finance. A Small Island Developing State is geographically defined, cannot diversify its cashflows across geography, aggregates small shocks that individuals absorb separately, has thin access to insurance, and falls back on grants and bailouts as its core risk management strategy, which then shows up in the price it pays to borrow. That is your description of a US county, scaled up and moved offshore. I had been treating the high cost of capital in these markets as a climate finance problem particular to developing economies. Reading your municipal work made me think it is a more general problem about undiversifiable, insurance-poor borrowers, and that the international version may have more to learn from the muni-bond market than from the climate funds.
That reading also gives me a formal vocabulary for the multiplicative form. In your Panama Canal paper with Mani Rouhi Rad, Vic Adamowicz, Alicia Entem and Patrick Lloyd-Smith, you distinguish the capital space from the services space and show that stocks can be complements while the flows they produce are substitutes. Climate finance is usually modelled as though institutional quality and deployed capital are substitutes, so that enough money compensates for weak institutions. My survey says otherwise, and the partial identification approach in that paper is the most promising way I have found to test the claim formally.
The collapse behaviour in the IRC has a precedent in your work as well. Your paper with Edward Tekwa, Simon Levin and Malin Pinsky shows that institutional path dependence on its own can produce alternative stable states, so that similar institutions end up trapped in very different but predictable outcomes. That is close to what my interviews described. Two countries with comparable fund access and technical capacity settle into different equilibria, and practitioners explain the difference by history rather than by any current policy difference. Your model outperformed competing explanations on a large dataset, and applying that approach to climate finance institutions is one of the things I most want to do at Yale.
Your Science paper on bats and white-nose syndrome sets up a comparison I want to run. It shows that biodiversity loss raises county borrowing costs, and that targeted investment in existing municipal bonds, paired with restoration, could pay for conservation and return a profit. Your argument that conservation finance should use existing market infrastructure where it can gives my work a clear benchmark. My layered capital structure is a new instrument, with a concessional first loss position, a multilateral guarantee mezzanine and a household or bank deposit senior tranche. The test is whether it lowers borrowing costs by more than the same concessional money would inside the sovereign and subnational debt markets that already exist, and that is a comparison I would like to make with you.
The third strand of the research is regenerative agriculture, and here your work reframed a conversation I had already had. I worked with Verra’s VM0042 methodology for improved agricultural land management while structuring a paddy cultivation carbon programme at Kangara Holdings. The additionality test I ran with the Sri Lankan government was a difference in differences comparison of adopters and nonadopters of the proposed practice changes, checking whether each intervention exceeded the 5 percent quantitative change threshold and whether regional adoption stayed below the 20 percent common practice ceiling. The farmers I sat across from in Sri Lanka’s dry zone were not thinking about additionality. They wanted to know what happens to their land rights if the project outlasts the company that signed the contract. Your paper with Kevin Berry and Brian Robinson on the ecological insurance trap helped me think about that question. Where financial insurance is missing, people build self-insurance out of the resource base itself, so an intervention that changes the resource base can remove the insurance while appearing to add value. A carbon contract that reorganizes land management and then expires is doing something structurally similar.
To keep the work tied to data, I plan to run a small pilot with a commercial bank in a Small Island Developing State during the doctorate. Dr. Pradeep Kurukulasuriya at UNCDF, Jason Spensley at the World Bank GEF and Dr. Anthony Miller at UN Sustainable Stock Exchanges have all seen early versions of the model, and Dr. Kurukulasuriya pushed me to treat how capital is raised and where it ends up going as linked problems. The pilot would produce real pricing, take-up and default data to discipline the model’s parameters. The natural capital and dynamic systems strands of this programme are where your supervision would matter most, Professor Fenichel.

title: Fund design, pilots and political economy
text:
Research / Statements / Fund design, pilots and political economy


Research statement for the PhD programme in Environmental Economics, Yale School of the Environment, Fall 2027. Written with reference to the work of Professor Matthew Kotchen.



My MSc dissertation at London Metropolitan University asked why climate finance reaches so few of the places that need it. It ended with a theoretical contribution I call the Institutional Reinforcement Cycle (IRC). I want to spend my doctoral years at Yale turning the IRC from a framework I believe in into something a skeptical economist would accept. That means writing it down formally, estimating it, and finding out where it fails. Your work on how multilateral funds choose and finance projects, Professor Kotchen, is the closest body of research to that problem that I have found.
The IRC treats a climate finance system as a product of its components rather than a sum. Institutional collaboration, policy alignment, blended finance deployment and transparency compound, so a value near zero on one of them can stall the whole system however much capital sits in the funds. My evidence so far is a survey of 103 climate finance professionals and eight interviews with practitioners at UNDP, UNCDF, UN Sustainable Stock Exchanges, FAO, the African Development Bank, the Asian Development Bank, the World Bank GEF, a central bank and a private capital firm. It points to institutional collaboration, rather than the volume of blended finance, as the binding constraint. I presented this at the 3rd International Conference on Biomimicry for Sustainability in August 2026, and the paper is now under revision at Climate and Development. A survey of this size motivates the multiplicative form but does not identify it, and getting to an estimable, identified specification is the first thing I would like to work on with you.
The finding I most want to test against your work is that the volume of blended finance is not the binding constraint. Your paper with Andrew Vogt reaches a related conclusion from a different direction. Using project data from the Global Environment Facility and the Green Climate Fund, you show that adding cofinancing objectives to a fund that already seeks to maximize its environmental impact is redundant at best and more likely counterproductive, and that cofinancing targets do little for realized environmental benefits. My survey reached a similar place from the practitioner side. The question your paper leaves open, and the one my framework is trying to answer, is what a fund should target instead when institutional collaboration is the scarce input. Your earlier work with Neeraj Negi on 3,269 GEF projects is the evidence base I would most like to learn to work with in trying to answer it.
Your work also gives my pilot a second role. I plan to run a small pilot with a commercial bank in a Small Island Developing State during the doctorate, designed to produce real pricing, take-up and default data to discipline the model. Your paper with Christopher Costello separates pilot projects, whose main purpose is information about whether a project is worth doing, from full projects at scale, and finds that pilots are often the better target for public subsidy. That changes what the concessional first loss tranche in my structure is for. If the first round of concessional capital is mainly buying information, it may be better sized and priced as an option on a later full project than as a standing subsidy, and I would like to work out what that implies for the rest of the structure. Dr. Pradeep Kurukulasuriya at UNCDF, Jason Spensley at the World Bank GEF and Dr. Anthony Miller at UN Sustainable Stock Exchanges have all seen early versions of the model. Mr. Spensley thought it technically feasible but politically uncertain, which is itself a reason to learn cheaply before committing at scale.
I also want to formalize the selection question. My structure pairs central bank regulated climate deposits with multilateral guarantees, and a guarantee facility may draw in the projects that would have been financed anyway while leaving the risky ones unfunded. In that case the concessional capital buys very little additional investment, which is the additionality problem moved up from the project to the fund. Your time as Deputy Assistant Secretary for Environment and Energy at the Treasury means you have seen from inside the institutions what my survey respondents described from outside them. The frustration that recurred across my data was that fund governance tracks donor convenience more closely than recipient need. That is a political economy problem before it is a finance problem, and I would like to model it as one.
The third strand of the research is regenerative agriculture. I worked with Verra’s VM0042 methodology for improved agricultural land management while structuring a carbon programme at Kangara Holdings. The additionality test I ran with the Sri Lankan government was a difference in differences comparison of adopters and nonadopters of the proposed practice changes, checking whether each intervention exceeded the 5 percent quantitative change threshold and whether regional adoption stayed below the 20 percent common practice ceiling. The farmers I sat across from in the dry zone were not thinking about additionality. They wanted to know what happens to their land rights if the project outlasts the company that signed the contract. That is an enforcement problem inside a voluntary market, and your work with Kathleen Segerson on group performance and group rights in resource management is where I would start to model it.
This work sits inside a wider programme with three strands, the capital structure itself, its application to energy and its application to regenerative agriculture. I have attended three UNFCCC COPs and two UNCCD COPs, and in those rooms the gap between capital pledged and capital deployed was the most consistent problem I saw. The fund design and political economy strands of this programme are where your work matters most to mine, Professor Kotchen, and I want to find out early where my framework holds and where it breaks.
